narrative:
The model estimated your chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt at 54.6 percent. Because that is greater than 50 percent, the school viewed you as a risk and denied your application. Three pieces of information drove that decision.

The most influential factor was your class standing in your third year of law school. You were in the second decile, which puts you among the lowest-performing students in your class. In comparison, accepted applicants typically sit around the sixth decile. This low rank strongly pushed the prediction toward failing the bar exam and was the main reason for the denial.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second strongest factor. Although your GPA of 2.60 is well below the accepted-student average of about 3.2, the model actually treated this factor as slightly helpful, nudging you toward passing. It softened the risk from your class rank by a small amount.

The third factor was family income. Your family is in the high-income bracket, a group that makes up only about 9 percent of accepted applicants. The model associated this with a lower chance of failure, so it also nudged the prediction slightly toward passing.

Even with those two supportive signals, your third-year class rank outweighed them, leaving your overall failure chance above 50 percent.

To strengthen a future application, focus on raising your academic performance to improve your class standing. You might also consider retaking the LSAT to demonstrate stronger potential. If you can show upward grade momentum and a higher LSAT score, you would present a much stronger case for admission.
